name: Example: Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Is Attained Over an Ellipse
problem: Find the minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x})=16x_1^2+16x_1x_2+x_2^2$ given that $16x_1^2 + x_2^2=16,$ and find the vector $\mathbf{x}$ at which the minimum is obtained.
worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14077353/assets/fab48c5c9c4d9adee4f270c6138d0f69317cfa59ad9d6f5dab2d4cad15d368c6.png)

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\dfrac{x_1^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{x_2^2}{4^2}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=1$ (along the $x_1$-axis) and $b=4$ (along the $x_2$-axis). 

If we introduce new variables

$\qquad$ $y_1={x_1} \quad$ and $\quad y_2 = \dfrac{x_2}{4},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into $y_1^2+y_2^2 = 1,$ or $\|\mathbf{y}\|=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14077353/assets/3042cf8eadb699a70b70daced51411fa570ec9cdf3b7b270943fe790739a5364.png) 

we obtain that $\mathbf{x} = P \mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = (P\mathbf{y})^T A \, (P\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{y}^T \! (P^TAP) \mathbf{y}= Q'(\mathbf{y}).
$$

As a result, since $P^T=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}16 & 8 \\ 8 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 8 \\ 32 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 32 \\ 32 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimise $Q'(\mathbf{y})$ when $\| \mathbf{y} \|=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}16-\lambda  & 32 \\ 32 & 16-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (16-\lambda )(16-\lambda )-1\,024 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-32\lambda -768 & =0 \\ (\lambda -48)(\lambda +16) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =48,\,-16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\min \{ Q'(\mathbf{y}) \: | \: \| \mathbf{y} \|=1 \} = \lambda_{\textrm{min}} = -16.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{\textrm{min}}=-16{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-16I) & =[\begin{aligned}16 & 32 \\ 32 & 16\end{aligned}]+16[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}32 & 32 \\ 32 & 32\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-16I))\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14077353/assets/df1ad3d9484608d37e762f74d2a61776c8f82f8eb650dcb0a37f47c5037678c4.png) Dividing $\mathbf{v}$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14077353/assets/c869aa1eb73c078eaac66201b1062b2d55a45d90ec2010b6af532ca601498a53.png) 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
